rationale: A wins because it is tighter and more disciplined about what the founder can actually defend. Its strongest line, "How AI actually shrinks a company: Klarna froze hiring and let attrition cut head count 20%," turns the ugliest fact into a real labor story and immediately names the proof gap. B has good shapes, but "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" puts words in the facts' mouth; the update says Klarna will not split roles cut versus roles left unfilled, not that jobs were cut and replaced by AI. That is how an accountability angle becomes its own accountability problem.
gaps_in_A: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" overclaims. The update says average customer-service chat resolution fell below two minutes; it does not say disputes specifically are resolved that fast or correctly.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is plausible, but not grounded in the supplied facts. If you make that claim, bring receipts or cut it.

"public markets pay a premium for AI head-count reduction" is a sharp markets frame, but it needs care: the update says profitable and filed to go public, not that the filing or investor narrative already centers AI efficiency.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" is the worst overreach in either set. The fact is roles cut versus left unfilled; "jobs it cut" and "replaced by AI" are not established.
"The most-mocked category of enterprise AI" is unsupported color. It may be true in the discourse, but it is not in the update and reads like a columnist's flourish looking for evidence.

"Klarna's profitability narrative leans on AI-driven cost reduction" goes beyond the facts. The company is profitable and has filed to go public; the set needs the prospectus before saying what the narrative leans on.

The fifth angle adds distinctness, but it also pads the set with a trend frame that depends on outside claims about chatbot reputation and ROI debate. Useful, but shakier than the labor, IPO, data, and consumer-protection stories.
